content: Very preterm infants often require respiratory support, which increases their risk of developing chronic lung disease and later neurodevelopmental disabilities. Methylxanthines, such as caffeine, aminophylline, and theophylline, are commonly used to prevent and treat apnea of prematurity and to facilitate extubation. However, there is ongoing uncertainty regarding the benefits and potential harms of different types of methylxanthines. The primary objective of this analysis was to evaluate the effects of methylxanthines on the incidence of apnea, death, neurodevelopmental disability, and other long-term outcomes in preterm infants who are either at risk for or already experiencing apnea, or who are undergoing extubation. The analysis included randomized controlled trials comparing methylxanthines to placebo or no treatment for these indications. A total of 18 studies involving 2,705 preterm infants were included. These studies assessed the use of methylxanthines for various indications: one study for any indication, six studies for the prevention of apnea, five studies for the treatment of apnea, and six studies for the prevention of re-intubation. Death or Major Neurodevelopmental Disability (DMND) at 18 to 24 Months The Caffeine for Apnea of Prematurity (CAP) trial, which enrolled 2,006 infants, was the only study to report on the composite outcome of death or major neurodevelopmental disability (DMND) at 18 to 24 months. Caffeine likely reduced the risk of DMND in preterm infants treated for any indication (risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78 to 0.97; risk difference [RD] -0.06, 95% CI -0.10 to -0.02; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] 16, 95% CI 10 to 50; moderate-certainty evidence). When analyzed based on specific treatment indications, caffeine likely had little or no effect on DMND in infants treated for the prevention of apnea (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.24; RD -0.00, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.09; moderate-certainty evidence). However, caffeine probably slightly reduced the risk of DMND in infants treated for apnea of prematurity (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.00; NNTB 16, 95% CI 7 to >1000; moderate-certainty evidence) and in those treated to prevent re-intubation (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.99; RD -0.08, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.00; NNTB 12, 95% CI 6 to >1000; moderate-certainty evidence). Death Across all studies, methylxanthine treatment for any indication likely resulted in little or no difference in the risk of death at hospital discharge (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.37; RD -0.00, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.02; moderate-certainty evidence). Major Neurodevelopmental Disability at 18 to 24 Months In the CAP trial, caffeine likely reduced the risk of major neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.96; RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.10 to -0.02; NNTB 16, 95% CI 10 to 50; moderate-certainty evidence). This included a significant reduction in the risk of cerebral palsy or gross motor disability (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.88; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.05 to -0.01; NNTB 33, 95% CI 20 to 100; moderate-certainty evidence) and a marginal reduction in the risk of developmental delay (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.00; RD -0.05, 95% CI -0.09 to -0.00; NNTB 20, 95% CI 11 to >1000; moderate-certainty evidence). Apneic Episodes and Ventilation Needs Methylxanthine treatment likely reduced the occurrence of any apneic episodes (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.52; RD -0.38, 95% CI -0.51 to -0.25; NNTB 3, 95% CI 2 to 4; moderate-certainty evidence) and the failure to achieve a reduction in apnea episodes after two to seven days of treatment (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.70; RD -0.31, 95% CI -0.44 to -0.17; NNTB 3, 95% CI 2 to 6; moderate-certainty evidence). It may also reduce the need for positive-pressure ventilation after treatment initiation (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.96; RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.01; NNTB 16, 95% CI 9 to 100; low-certainty evidence). Chronic Lung Disease Methylxanthine treatment significantly reduced the risk of chronic lung disease, defined as the need for supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.85; RD -0.10, 95% CI -0.14 to -0.06; NNTB 10, 95% CI 7 to 16; high-certainty evidence). Extubation and Re-intubation Methylxanthine treatment for the prevention of re-intubation likely resulted in a substantial reduction in failed extubation compared to no treatment (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.71; RD -0.27, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.15; NNTB 4, 95% CI 2 to 6; moderate-certainty evidence). Conclusion Caffeine likely reduces the risk of death, major neurodevelopmental disability, and the composite outcome of DMND at 18 to 24 months in preterm infants. Methylxanthine treatment for any indication likely reduces the risk of apneic episodes, failed apnea reduction, cerebral palsy, developmental delay, and may reduce the need for positive-pressure ventilation. Additionally, methylxanthines significantly reduce the risk of chronic lung disease and improve extubation success rates.
